facts.title: Named for Golden Gemstones
facts.text: Zirconium's name traces to the mineral zircon, whose name likely comes from the Persian word zargun, meaning 'gold-colored.' The German chemist Martin Heinrich Klaproth identified the new element inside zircon in 1789 while analyzing a gemstone from Sri Lanka. He could not isolate the pure metal, however, leaving that challenge for later chemists.

facts.title: First Isolated Impure in 1824
facts.text: The Swedish chemist Jöns Jacob Berzelius first isolated impure zirconium metal in 1824 by heating potassium with potassium zirconium fluoride. The result was a black powder rather than a shiny metal, because making pure, ductile zirconium is genuinely difficult. Reasonably pure metal was not produced until 1925, when Anton van Arkel and Jan de Boer perfected their iodide crystal-bar process.

facts.title: The Nuclear Reactor Metal
facts.text: Zirconium is prized in nuclear reactors because it barely absorbs the neutrons that sustain a chain reaction, while resisting corrosion from hot, high-pressure water. Most reactor fuel rods are clad in a zirconium alloy called Zircaloy. A typical reactor core contains many tonnes of the metal wrapped around its uranium fuel pellets.

facts.title: Hafnium, Its Hidden Twin
facts.text: Zirconium almost always occurs alongside hafnium, an element so chemically similar that the two are among the hardest pairs to separate. This matters enormously for nuclear engineering, because hafnium is a strong neutron absorber and must be stripped out of reactor-grade zirconium. The same chemistry is then turned around to use that hafnium in reactor control rods.

facts.title: Diamond's Convincing Rival
facts.text: Cubic zirconia, the synthetic crystalline form of zirconium dioxide, is the most popular diamond simulant in jewelry. It is colorless, hard, and sparkles brilliantly, yet costs a tiny fraction of a real diamond. Because it is denser than diamond, a cubic zirconia stone of the same size feels noticeably heavier in the hand.

facts.title: A Ceramic That Bends Like Metal
facts.text: Zirconia ceramic is unusually tough for a ceramic thanks to a trick called transformation toughening, where tiny crystal grains change shape near a crack and squeeze it shut. This lets zirconia knives keep an exceptionally sharp edge and resist chipping. The same ceramic is used for durable dental crowns and artificial hip joints that the body tolerates well.

facts.title: Sparks That Once Lit Photos
facts.text: Finely powdered zirconium ignites readily and burns with an intense flash, releasing a great deal of light. This made it a key ingredient in early flashbulbs used by photographers before electronic flash units existed. The same energetic burning explains why zirconium powder must be handled carefully to avoid fires.

facts.title: Born in Dying Stars
facts.text: Zirconium is forged inside aging stars through the slow capture of neutrons by lighter atoms, a process astronomers call the s-process. Spectral lines of zirconium oxide are so prominent in certain cool giant stars that an entire class, called S-type stars, is partly defined by them. The element also turned up in the rocks and soil that Apollo astronauts brought back from the Moon.

facts.title: Abundant but Never Pure
facts.text: Zirconium is more common in Earth's crust than copper, zinc, or lead, making up roughly 130 parts per million. Despite that abundance, it is never found as a free metal in nature and always hides inside minerals, chiefly zircon and baddeleyite. Australia and South Africa supply much of the world's zircon, often as a byproduct of mining titanium-bearing sands.

facts.title: Ancient Crystals That Date Earth
facts.text: Tiny zircon crystals are remarkably tough and lock in trace uranium when they form, which slowly decays into lead at a known rate. By measuring that uranium-to-lead ratio, geologists read a zircon's age like a clock. The oldest known fragments of Earth's crust are zircon grains from the Jack Hills of Western Australia, dated to about 4.4 billion years.
